newsitem.title: UK: Ex-Bosnia mediator Owen urges new deal for UN.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Bosnia mediator Owen urges new deal for UN.

text.p: Former Bosnia peace mediator Lord Owen called on Tuesday for United Nations reform including restricting its secretary-general to a single, seven-year term.
With the United States opposed to the reappointment of Boutros Boutros-Ghali to a second and final five-year term, Owen said President Bill Clinton should be ready to compromise.

"President Clinton, newly elected, would gain greatly in international stature if he placed five Security Council reforms at the top of his priorities," Owen said in a lecture delivered in the university city of Oxford.

Owen proposed increasing Security Council membership, making membership conditional on being prepared to commit troops to a U.N. peace force, ensuring the secretary-general cannot be a national of a permanent Security Council member, and reducing the U.S. contribution to the U.N. budget.
A seven-year, non-renewable term for the secretary-general would avoid re-election manoeuvring and allow Boutros-Ghali to serve as the first seven-year U.N. chief, Owen said.
The Clinton administration has vowed to block the Egyptian diplomat's bid for a second term, saying he has not done enough to reform the world body.
Washington can veto Boutros-Ghali's re-election bid, but any successor it chooses would almost certainly be opposed by other key members.
Owen, a former British foreign secretary, confirmed that Boutros-Ghali had been offered a face-saving 12-month extension to his term of office.
"In the bargaining that went on before the Americans announced their veto, Boutros was offered an extra year.

"But the Americans were reluctant to offer two years and were not sure that Boutros, having announced that he would only stand for one term initially, might not actually go and instead serve a second five year term," Owen said.
Owen said Germany, India and Japan should be made permanent Security Council members, but without the veto enjoyed by the present five -- the U.S., Russia, China, Britain and France.

Six more countries could also be added to the 15-member council on the basis of population, gross domestic product, political weight and size -- Brazil, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan and, by rotation, two out of Egypt, South Africa and Nigeria.
A condition of council membership should be a commitment to contribute 1,000 troops for a U.N. rapid reaction force.

As a means of reducing the U.N.'s dependence on "one major superpower", the percentage of its budget contributed by the U.S. should be cut immediately from 30 percent to 20 percent, with 10 percent a long-term objective, Owen said.
The U.S. owes the U.N. more than $1.4 billion in past dues and for peacekeeping operations.
